newsitem.title: USA: Flood-ravaged U.S. plains to get federal aid.
newsitem.headline: Flood-ravaged U.S. plains to get federal aid.

text.p: Flood-stricken residents of this submerged city cheered President Bill Clinton's pledge on Tuesday of more federal aid to help them rebuild when floodwaters from swollen rivers finally recede.

Clinton, awed by the extent of damage during an aerial tour, promised the federal government would pay for all emergency efforts and said he would ask Congress to approve an additional $200 million in long-term aid.
That would provide a total of $488 million for the battered states of North Dakota, South Dakota and Minnesota, most of which he had previously declared disaster areas.
"We're going to need even more," said Sen. Kent Conrad, a North Dakota Democrat. Some local officials have suggested flood damage may be more than $1 billion.

With the Grand Forks water treatment plant inundated by floodwaters contaminated by raw sewage and dead animals, residents may not be able to return home for weeks. They then face a massive task of cleaning up and rebuilding.

Clinton suggested in discussions with local officials that trailer homes be brought in at federal expense to house residents during the cleanup, but water and other services need to be restored first.

Telephone service was being maintained by a team of workers pumping out water from a downtown switching station surrounded by floodwaters. Several department stores managed to reopen on Tuesday for a few hours, and dikes were being built to hold back any further river surges.

After his helicopter tour, Clinton was greeted by cheering crowds at Grand Forks Air Force Base 15 miles (24 km) west of the city, where 2,500 of the 45,000 people who evacuated Grand Forks are living in a cavernous airplane hanger.
The rest, along with 9,000 residents from East Grand Forks, Minnesota, have found shelter with friends, relatives, or compassionate strangers who have opened their homes.
Clinton urged flood victims to maintain their "spirit and faith that ... water cannot wash away, fire cannot burn away and a blizzard cannot freeze away.
"And if you don't give it away, it will bring you back better than ever and we'll be with you every step of the way," he said to cheers.

After his brief remarks, Clinton shook hands with dozens of people, hugging some of them. Clinton told one group of volunteers, "Thank you for being here," prompting an elderly man to shout back, "Thanks for coming."

Earlier, Clinton marvelled at the damage wrought by the raging Red River, which remained at its 54 foot (16.4 metre) crest at Grand Forks, and a weekend fire that burned unchecked for hours and left 11 downtown buildings gutted.
"I don't recall ever in my life seeing anything like this," he said. It was "not an ordinary disaster, if there is such a thing."
An unprecedented parade of winter storms, followed by a spring thaw and an early April ice storm triggered flooding across three states, forcing thousands to flee their homes.

The Red River that runs northward into Canada broadened its path on the flat floodplain, threatening rural towns and eventually could endanger the Canadian provincial capital of Winnipeg, a city of 630,000.
Canada's Manitoba province declared a state of emergency as more than 3,200 residents were ordered to quit their homes, and 20,000 more were warned of possible evacuation.
In the first death related to the Red River flooding, a four-year-old boy living in a Hutterite colony near Portage-la-Prairie, Manitoba, drowned in a culvert.
The catastrophe has cut all land links between Minnesota and North Dakota along a 150-mile (240 km) stretch from Fargo, North Dakota, to the Canadian border.
